original_question: For cyclic groups Z_n, determine whether the known lower bounds for the three-term restricted critical number chi_hat(Z_n, 3) are always sharp. More precisely, if n has a prime divisor congruent to 2 mod 3 and p is the smallest such divisor, does chi_hat(Z_n, 3) always equal (1 + 1/p)n/3 + 3 when n = p, (1 + 1/p)n/3 + 2 when n = 3p, and (1 + 1/p)n/3 + 1 otherwise? If n has no prime divisor congruent to 2 mod 3, does chi_hat(Z_n, 3) always equal floor(n/3) + 4 when 9 divides n and floor(n/3) + 3 otherwise?
target_in_paper: Section 0.6 ("Critical numbers"), specifically the unnumbered open problem immediately after the displayed lower bounds for \widehat{\chi}(\mathbb{Z}_n,3), where the paper says that the author believes equality holds in those bounds for all n.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the exact object under discussion— the restricted 3-critical number of the cyclic group \mathbb{Z}_n — and it reproduces the paper’s full piecewise case split and constants for the conjectured exact value: the branch according to whether n has a prime divisor congruent to 2 mod 3, the role of the smallest such prime p, the exceptional subcases n=p and n=3p, and the alternative branch when no prime divisor of n is congruent to 2 mod 3, including the 9\mid n versus 9\nmid n distinction.
missing_details: The draft does not define \widehat{\chi}(\mathbb{Z}_n,3): it is the least integer m such that 3^\wedge A=\mathbb{Z}_n for every m-element subset A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}_n.
The draft does not define the restricted three-fold sumset 3^\wedge A=\{a_1+a_2+a_3: a_1,a_2,a_3\in A\text{ are pairwise distinct}\}.
It should explicitly state that \mathbb{Z}_n is the cyclic group of order n written additively, as in the paper’s notation section.
It should make clear that the paper’s conjectural question is whether equality holds in the lower bounds stated just before it, not merely whether some lower bound is sharp in an unspecified sense.
For full paper-faithfulness, the open part should be scoped to the unresolved regime emphasized in the discussion: odd composite n (the paper notes that the prime and even cases are already known).
If one wants to match the source of the lower bounds exactly, one should mention that those bounds are stated there for n\ge 15, after which the paper conjectures equality in all cases discussed.
It should specify that p means the smallest prime divisor of n satisfying p\equiv 2 \pmod 3.
refined_question: Let \mathbb{Z}_n be the cyclic group of order n, written additively. For a subset A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}_n, define the restricted three-fold sumset by 3^\wedge A:=\{a_1+a_2+a_3:\ a_1,a_2,a_3\in A\text{ are pairwise distinct}\}, and let \widehat{\chi}(\mathbb{Z}_n,3) denote the least integer m such that 3^\wedge A=\mathbb{Z}_n for every m-element subset A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}_n. For the remaining unresolved odd composite cases (equivalently, for every n\ge 15 in the paper’s conjectural formulation), are the lower bounds from Section 0.6 always exact? That is: if n has a prime divisor congruent to 2 mod 3 and p is the smallest such prime, must one have \widehat{\chi}(\mathbb{Z}_n,3)=((1+1/p)n/3)+3 when n=p, \widehat{\chi}(\mathbb{Z}_n,3)=((1+1/p)n/3)+2 when n=3p, and \widehat{\chi}(\mathbb{Z}_n,3)=((1+1/p)n/3)+1 otherwise; and if n has no prime divisor congruent to 2 mod 3, must one have \widehat{\chi}(\mathbb{Z}_n,3)=\lfloor n/3\rfloor+4 when 9\mid n and \widehat{\chi}(\mathbb{Z}_n,3)=\lfloor n/3\rfloor+3 otherwise?
justification: Section 0.1 supplies the ambient notation: cyclic groups are identified with \mathbb{Z}_n, and h^\wedge A denotes the h-fold restricted sumset. Section 0.6 then defines restricted critical numbers and narrows attention to \widehat{\chi}(\mathbb{Z}_n,3). In that section the paper states the two piecewise lower bounds and immediately follows them with the claim that the author believes equality actually holds in all cases discussed. Your draft is therefore very close to the paper’s actual intent; it mainly needs the operator definitions and the exact quantifier/scope to become fully stand-alone and paper-faithful.
